title: The World of AI: Nonprofits and Open Source Foundations page
answer: This is a catalogue page from The World of AI listing four individually verified organisations under Nonprofits and Open Source Foundations, each with a sourced classification note. Its most useful point is that the four entries are two nonprofits and two open-source foundations touching AI tooling and evaluation, but none are infrastructure builders in the compute or power sense. LMSYS stewards Chatbot Arena, Khan Academy is an AI end-user in education, and Krita and Blender steward creative software. The page warns it does not cover training compute providers, standards bodies, or open-model foundations.

sections.body: The World of AI publishes this catalogue page, titled Nonprofits and Open Source Foundations, as part of its AI ecosystem section. It is a short directory entry, not a report or article, and it states that it lists four individually verified organisations, each with a sourced classification note. The page says every entry carries the source that decided it and the date that source was last read. The citation line gives a retrieval date of 26 September 2026. The page also describes the wider site as rebuilt daily from primary sources and carrying the date it was last verified.
sections.heading: What this source is

sections.body: The page groups four organisations under nonprofits and open source foundations stewarding models, standards, and shared infrastructure, with governance model and funding. It says the four are two nonprofits and two open-source foundations with roles that touch AI tooling and evaluation, but none are infrastructure builders in the compute or power sense. LMSYS is described as the most directly AI-central entry because it stewards Chatbot Arena, a shared evaluation platform the broader AI community uses to benchmark model quality. The page argues this neutral, open evaluation infrastructure matters because model comparison depends on it, yet it sits outside the commercial incentives of the labs being evaluated. Khan Academy is called an end-user of AI capability in education, not a producer of it. The Krita Foundation and Blender Foundation steward creative software tools that AI-generated imagery and 3D content increasingly intersect with, but their primary missions predate and are not defined by AI. The page stresses that classifications are made one at a time against a document the organisation published about itself, with the document recorded, and that nothing was assigned by keyword, by a model, or by inheritance from a parent company. It says a classification that keeps no evidence cannot be audited and a wrong one survives quietly.
sections.heading: What it says

sections.body: The source gives one main number: four individually verified organisations. It defines the group as two nonprofits and two open-source foundations. It names LMSYS, Khan Academy, the Krita Foundation, and the Blender Foundation. It states that none are infrastructure builders in the compute or power sense. It says the notes confirm only organizational structure and nonprofit status, not funding scale, compute access, or governance detail. It also states that no training compute providers, no standards bodies setting grid or data-center specifications, and no open-model foundations releasing weights appear in this list.
sections.heading: Figures and claims worth noting

sections.body: A reader following AI in nonprofits can use this page as a small, sourced starting point for identifying nonprofit and open-source organisations whose work touches AI tooling and evaluation. It is most useful for seeing how the sector is classified and for understanding that the page's own scope is narrow. It points to LMSYS and Chatbot Arena as shared evaluation infrastructure, to Khan Academy as an education end-user, and to Krita and Blender as creative software stewards. It also makes clear that anyone looking for nonprofit involvement in compute, power, standards, or open model weights will need other sources.
sections.heading: What it means for AI in Nonprofits

sections.body: The page is explicit that its coverage is partial. It has only four entries, and it says the notes confirm only organizational structure and nonprofit status, not funding scale, compute access, or governance detail. It does not cover training compute providers, standards bodies setting grid or data-center specifications, or open-model foundations that release weights for public use. It is a catalogue page rather than a full analysis, and the surrounding site promotes books, consulting services, audits, and a novel, so it is not a neutral academic publication. The retrieval date is 26 September 2026, and the page says the wider site is rebuilt daily, but this entry remains a short directory note.
